**Ch 004 draft — checking for structural damage**

**"The juxtaposition of these two remarks was startling."**
The draft has replaced the Rosy Rosenthal scene with: *"Wolfshiem reminisced about old gangland murders at the Metropole."* Then comes Wolfshiem's line about a "business gonnegtion," followed by: "The juxtaposition of these two remarks was startling." This is a broken pivot — the sentence explicitly announces a *juxtaposition* between two specific remarks, but the first of the two remarks (Wolfshiem's specific Rosenthal murder story ending with "Five, with Becker") has been reduced to a narrative summary. The source's logic is: murder anecdote → business proposition = shocking juxtaposition. The draft's summary gives a reader the gist of gangland talk, so "startling" is not *inexplicable*, but the word "juxtaposition" signals that two discrete quoted or paraphraseable remarks sit side-by-side — and only one of them is present as a remark. A competent reader would be confused about what specifically is being juxtaposed, because the first element has been dissolved into indirect narration while the pivot word treats it as a discrete statement. This clears the gate test.

**"Gatsby bought that house so that Daisy would be just across the bay. / Then it had not been merely the stars to which he had aspired on that June night."**
The draft never establishes Gatsby staring at a green light or reaching toward stars on any June night. The source's Ch 001 draft (not provided here but the Ch 004 source's own Jordan Baker section ends without this either; this phrase originates in Ch 001 where Gatsby reaches toward a distant light). Checking: does the Ch 004 *draft* contain any reference to "the stars" or a June night aspiration? No. However, examining the authorized cuts list — Ch 001 material was cut, but the green-light/star-reaching scene is not listed as an authorized cut. This is a dangling reference: "the stars to which he had aspired on that June night" has no antecedent in the preceding draft. A reader who has only the draft would have no idea what stars or which June night is meant.

**Ch 004 draft — Jordan section: "One October day in nineteen-seventeen — (said Jordan Baker that afternoon, sitting up very straight on a straight chair in the tea-garden at the Plaza Hotel) —"**
The sentence trails off with a dash and never completes. In the source, the dash leads directly into Jordan's narrative: "I was walking along from one place to another…" In the draft the opening parenthetical is followed by a new paragraph beginning "The largest of the banners…" — so the main clause of the sentence ("One October day… I was walking along…") is simply absent. The sentence as printed has no main clause; it opens a subordinate construction that is never completed. A reader cannot parse this as a standalone sentence. This is non-parseable.

**Ch 005 draft — "Gatsby called for the boarder to play the piano"**
The draft uses the definite noun phrase "the boarder" with the definite article, treating it as an established identity. Checking the Ch 005 draft's own preceding text: there is no prior introduction of any boarder or of Klipspringer. The source introduced him in the tour of the house: *"It was Mr. Klipspringer, the 'boarder.' I had seen him wandering hungrily about the beach that morning."* This passage was cut from the draft (the upstairs tour passage was compressed and the boarder's appearance removed). "The boarder" in the draft has no antecedent anywhere in the Ch 005 draft. Klipspringer is on the authorized minor-character removal list, but the removal of his introduction while retaining "the boarder" as a definite reference is a seam that is *not* merely residual from the authorized cut — the drafter was expected to either remove the piano scene or replace "the boarder" with a neutral phrase. A reader encounters "the boarder" with zero prior context and cannot identify who this is. This clears the gate test as a genuine dangling reference.

**Ch 005 draft — "Before I could answer further, Daisy came out of the house"**
The source has: *"Do you mean you've been thinking over what I proposed the other night?"* / *"Before I could answer, Daisy came out…"* The draft cuts Gatsby's question about the side-business proposal, so "Before I could answer further" implies a question was just asked in the draft that was not. Looking at the draft: Gatsby says "I was in the drug business and then I was in the oil business. But I'm not in either one now." There is no pending question requiring an answer. "Before I could answer further" is a broken pivot — it presupposes an interrupted reply, but nothing in the preceding draft called for one. A reader would be confused about what Nick was about to answer.
